notes: Pinned tools and data that close the local CTF tool gaps of the ctf-kali runtime.
Hashes for ysoserial, marshalsec, JNDI-Injection-Exploit and StegSolve are the ones the upstream muteki worker Dockerfile (docker/worker/Dockerfile) pins; our downloaded bytes match them exactly.
Installed inside ctf-kali; the Muteki tool root exposes them through ./toolbox/bin wrappers.

assets.name: foundry
assets.install: /opt/ctf/foundry (forge, cast, anvil, solar; foundry's own chisel is exposed as fchisel)

assets.name: chisel-target-binaries
assets.note: The Kali package provides the tunnel client; these are the static binaries uploaded to a controlled target.

assets.name: bkcrack
assets.note: Known-plaintext attack on ZipCrypto archives; replaces the unmaintained pkcrack the playbooks name.

assets.name: cfr
assets.repository: leibnitz27/cfr (jar published to Maven Central as org.benf:cfr)
assets.note: JVM bytecode decompiler; jadx covers Android and ilspycmd covers .NET, CFR covers plain .class/.jar.

assets.name: kerbrute
assets.note: AD username enumeration and pre-auth (AS-REP) brute forcing; the corpora describe the technique, this is what performs it.

assets.name: openstego
assets.note: LSB steganography for PNG/JPEG; the smoke test embeds and recovers a message to prove the jar works.

batch5_basis.why: Same audit method, second candidate sweep: AD credential tooling, kernel-pwn symbol recovery, PE parsing and stego details that the first sweep did not cover. Every entry was verified to be absent before it was added, and each addition has a functional check in scripts/smoke-tools.sh.
notable: kerbrute enumerates and pre-auth-brutes AD usernames, which the corpus describes but the image could not do
pypykatz parses LSASS dumps and registry hives offline, the Linux-side counterpart of mimikatz
vmlinux-to-elf turns a stripped bzImage into a symbolised ELF, the entry point of every kernel-pwn challenge
diec + pefile cover packer/PE identification; openstego is proven by an embed/extract round trip

batch4_basis.why: The gap list comes from auditing the tool names the CTF playbooks themselves reference, not from guessing: scripts/playbook-tool-audit.sh prints what is named but not callable, and scripts/smoke-tools.sh runs each replacement on a real input before it counts as done.
notable: tesseract closes the 'flag is text rendered into an image' gap (the forensics-pcapin class of task)
volatility3 is what the playbooks call vol3; the launcher keeps that name
fpylll is the lattice/LLL solver behind most modern RSA-CTF attacks
hashpumpy and bkcrack cover hash length extension and known-plaintext ZIP
wabt and multimon-ng cover WASM and RF/audio challenges

pip_repairs.why: Installing the cloud/AD tool set into the shared core venv downgraded pydantic to 1.x and z3-solver to 4.13, which broke fastapi/mcp/web3 and angr; claripy and arpy were also missing. Re-applying these pins after any bulk pip install keeps the venv usable.
verified: claripy.BVS solver returns the expected value

skipped.name: garak / pyrit
skipped.reason: AI/LLM-security stack pulls the torch/transformers tree; the install failed inside the shared core venv and its value for classic CTF categories is low. Install into a dedicated venv if LLM-security challenges appear.
